doc.title: Chuck Lamb interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 7, 2023

chapter: Learning, living and the Colorado years
title: Rowe visits the band house to teach theory
summary: Rowe recalls visiting the young band, who played by ear; they discuss learning by ear versus music school.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: What was the other, after Dry Jack the — I have to insert one thing because this stuck in my head, for our viewers, I was teaching at the school they you had sort of recently graduated from, at Vernon, Verona, Sherrill and you guys were together pre Inner City and you asked me to come over to this house where you were all living I think cause you wanted to learn some, I don’t know what it was, theory.

Rich. My brother Rich. I told you he said to say hi and he said, “Oh man, Monk, that’s great.” But he said, “Do you remember he came over to the house to teach us” Rich said he came over to teach us theory. And I remember you coming over and hanging. I just remember you were a really cool guy and we had a lot of fun. But you know Rich said, “Yeah” though, our history man is pretty cool.
I said, “Play a tune for me you guys.”

And when it was over I said, “What the hell do you want me to show you?” It was great. Because when I got out of college I had this bit of an attitude that people who didn’t also go to college and study music were somewhat lesser musicians. And then I learned along the way that people who learned by ear had a whole other thing that I didn’t have and that it’s very valuable. And sometimes in composing they think of things to do chord-wise or whatever-wise, that schooled musicians wouldn’t think of, or would think of and dismiss.

You know that was part of the discussion about, you know with my peers about not going to school. They’re going, “Man who knows what that would have done to your creative spirit” which you know just what you’re saying. I understand that that might have dampened it, to get too theoretical and too into the learning thing, and take away from the improv-ability but then again I don’t think I would have been deterred by anything you know, I would have just enjoyed the knowledge coming at me. And I remember our guitar player at that time, because Rich told me that, I can’t say I remember, Rich said that the guitar player in the band when you came over, he was like, “I don’t want to learn anything. I just want to keep doing this. Why are we trying to learn stuff?” That was so great of you to come over man. And, you know, because you were a well-respected player by us too so it was like wow man, this guy is like a serious musician. And you still are man, still a great player.
